extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of classical philosophy and literature (and writers studying character/archetype portrayals)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of a Plato Republic passage describing types of souls/governments, pleasures, and the origins and consequences of tyranny; useful for philosophical study or for writers seeking archetypal character models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of the tyrannical soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The tyrannical man is generated when a person, having been drawn first to moderate indulgence, then to lawless pleasure by corrupt company, has a 'master passion' (a monstrous winged drone) implanted that rules his soul; Madness becomes 'captain of his guard' and eradicates better principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs to look for: a progression from moderation to lawlessness under corrupt influence; emergence of a single dominating passion (often sexual/love-driven) that suppresses shame and temperance. Anti-pattern: treating tyranny as instantaneous rather than as a gradual capture of the soul by one ruling appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyrant as slave to love and appetites
rubrics_metrics.description: Love (and analogous passions) lives as 'lord of the house' within him, ordering the soul; desire becomes insatiable, revenues are spent, and the man is driven to fraud, plunder, and crime to satisfy endless wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral markers: escalating desires, financial ruin, resort to deception or force, prioritizing immediate pleasures over prior moral commitments. Use as a checklist when depicting or diagnosing a character's moral decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public tyranny arises from private tyrannical natures
rubrics_metrics.description: When many individuals of tyrannical character gather and become conscious of strength, they choose one among them who has most of the tyrant in his soul to be the public tyrant; private vice scales to public oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative implication: group dynamics amplify individual vices into political tyranny. Warning: don't separate private moral corruption from political outcomes when analyzing causes of tyrannies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and social role of the class allied to tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Those surrounding the tyrant (his retainers/body-guard) are thieves, burglars, informers, false witnesses, bribe-takers, man-stealers—small in number perhaps, but capable of great mischief and, when numerous, of producing a tyrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating a tyrant's milieu, include criminality, bribery, and informers; show how petty crimes and moral degradation provide the instrumentarium of tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyrant's internal condition: fear, isolation, and insecurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Although outwardly masterful, the tyrant is inwardly slave-like: full of fear, jealous, friendless, jealous of travel/experience, forced into adulation and servility, living like a hidden, jealous person rather than a free citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization tip: juxtapose external power with internal paralysis and paranoia. Anti-pattern: portraying absolute rulers as uniformly content or secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy between city-regimes and soul-types
rubrics_metrics.description: States and souls correspond: royal (kingly) maps to the best soul, timocratic/oligarchic/democratic/tyrannical map to middling to worst souls; to judge a soul's virtue and happiness, use the parallel with the kind of state it resembles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the city–soul analogy as an evaluative device—assess an individual's moral constitution by asking which regime's traits it mirrors. For writers: model characters on regime archetypes to explore moral consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripartite soul: reason, spirit, appetite
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul has three principles: the rational (lover of wisdom), the spirited/contentious (seeking honor/fame), and the appetitive (concerned with gain and bodily desires); each corresponds to particular pleasures and aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or constructing character motivations, identify which soul-part predominates and align their pleasures/aims accordingly (knowledge, honor, gain). Anti-pattern: treating a character as motivated by a single uncomplicated motive without internal conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for true pleasure (experience, wisdom, and reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best judge of pleasures is the lover of wisdom because he has the greatest experience of the different pleasures and possesses reason; pleasures approved by wisdom and reason are the truest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pleasures by appealing to wiser and more experienced perspectives rather than immediate appearances. In storytelling, privilege the long-view, intellectual perspective to adjudicate what is genuinely fulfilling vs illusory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between pure intellectual pleasures and bodily pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures derived from knowledge/truth are pure and abiding; many bodily pleasures are 'shadows' or 'reliefs of pain'—transient, mixed with pain, and often based on ignorance of truer goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to create contrasts between characters satisfied by learning/virtue versus those chasing sensual gratification; depict bodily pleasures as fleeting and often accompanied by regret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of truth/being as measure of pleasure's reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Things that partake more of invariable, immortal Being (truth, knowledge, mind, virtue) yield truer and more real pleasures than those concerned with the variable and mortal (food, drink, material gain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the 'reality' of a pleasure by how closely it connects to enduring truth or virtue. For creative work, craft stakes and rewards that contrast ephemeral satisfactions with deeper, more substantial joys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as internal harmony and its pleasurable outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: When the whole soul follows the philosophical principle (reason) so that the parts are just and do their own work, the person enjoys the best and truest pleasures appropriate to each part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use justice as a structural criterion: a character is flourishing when interior elements are harmonized. Plot/arc tip: moral growth can be shown as increasing internal order and corresponding deeper pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refutation of 'pleasure equals cessation of pain'
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all pleasures are mere cessation of pain; some (e.g., smell) appear without antecedent pain. The intermediate state (rest) may seem pleasant only in contrast; pure pleasure must be evaluated beyond comparative appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of simplistic accounts reducing pleasure to relief. In characterization, show moments where apparent satisfaction is only relief and not true fulfillment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative ranking of lives by scope of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosopher (lover of wisdom) has double experience—he taste other pleasures as well as intellectual ones—so he judges better and his life is the most pleasant; next the lover of honor, and last the lover of gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ranking characters' well-being or creating moral judgments within a narrative, consider breadth and depth of experience as a criterion: more reflective experience yields better judgment and truer pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifying the distance from true pleasure (metaphorically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato uses a numerical metaphor (three times three intervals leading to 729) to signify how vastly removed the tyrant's pleasures are from the king's—the greater the departure from reason and law, the more illusory and painful the pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphoric or hyperbolic measures to dramatize moral distance: extreme vice can be depicted as exponentially farther from true goods. Anti-pattern: portraying moral differences as only marginal when discussing profound ethical contrasts.
